title: Constant finite-field coefficients are dualizing on an excellent strictly henselian trait
statement: Let $R$ be an excellent strictly henselian discrete valuation ring, with $\ell$ invertible, and put $T=\operatorname{Spec}R$ [def-sc-discrete-valuation-ring, def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology, def-exc-excellent-ring]. Use the ordinary small-etale derived category of modules over the constant sheaf $A=\mathbf F_\ell$, for a prime $\ell$ [def-weil-pbc-derived-categories]. For $K$ in this category put $D_KM=R\mathcal Hom_A(M,K)$ [def-pur-derived-internal-hom]. In this statement, saying that $K$ is dualizing means exactly that $K\in D^b_c$, $D_K$ sends $D^b_c$ to $D^b_c$, and for every $M\in D^b_c$ the map $M\to D_K^2M$ transposed from evaluation after tensor symmetry is an isomorphism, naturally in $M$ [def-weil-pbc-constructible-complexes, def-kun-derived-tensor]. Then the constant rank-one sheaf $A_T$ in degree zero is dualizing on $T$.

source.place: Expose XVII, sections 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262: the exact tame-inertia supported-cohomology model, used with finite-dimensional F_ell modules and ordinary evaluation duality. This dimension-one assertion is independent of Theorem 0.9 and of potential dualizing complexes; completeness and mixed characteristic are not required.

proof.text: Write $i:s\hookrightarrow T$, $j:\eta\hookrightarrow T$, and $H,S,G$ as in the trait model. The gluing equivalence identifies a sheaf with $(W,V,a)$ and computes kernels and cokernels componentwise. For a constructible sheaf, $W$ and $V$ are finite-dimensional $A$-spaces. Conversely finite $W,V$ give constructibility on the two locally closed strata $s,\eta$: a finite continuous representation is trivialized by an etale cover, since a basis has an open common stabilizer, and the field etale/Galois-set equivalence supplies its covering orbit. Thus on this trait kernels, cokernels and extensions of finite-stalk sheaves are constructible, directly by finite-dimensional linear algebra. The constant sheaf has $W=V=A$ and is bounded constructible.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text:
Let $\mathscr L$ be a lisse finite-dimensional sheaf on $\eta$, with generic representation $V$. Put $W_0=V^S$, choose a topological generator $\sigma$ of $G$, and write $t=\sigma|_{W_0}$. The generic-boundary model, with coefficient exponent $n=1$, computes
$$C(V)=R\Gamma(\eta,\mathscr L)\simeq[W_0\xrightarrow{1-t}W_0]$$
in degrees $0,1$, using evaluation on $1-\sigma$. It also gives $R\Gamma(T,N)\simeq N_s$ for bounded-below $N$. Hence $i^*Rj_*\mathscr L=C(V)$: take an injective resolution on $\eta$; direct image preserves injectives because the exact open restriction is its left adjoint, and $\Gamma(T,j_*I)=\Gamma(\eta,I)$. On $\eta$, the same resolution restricts back to itself. Thus $Rj_*\mathscr L$ is bounded constructible: its closed cohomology is the kernel and cokernel of $1-t$, and its generic cohomology is $V$ in degree zero. The residue model for $A_T$ is $[A\xrightarrow{1}A\xrightarrow{0}\operatorname{Hom}_{A[[G]]}(I,A)]$. It follows that $E=Ri^!A_T\simeq A(-1)[-2]$, where the one-dimensional space $A(-1)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,A)$ is identified with the last term as in that model. Indeed on sheaves $i^!_0$ is the kernel of restriction, and on the separably closed $s$ global sections is the stalk; the same injective resolution computes both $Ri^!$ and supported sections.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text: The boundary $b:C(A)\to E[1]=A(-1)[-1]$ is an isomorphism on $H^1$. More precisely the generic-boundary model sends a degree-one class represented by $x\in\operatorname{Hom}_{A[[G]]}(I,A)$ to $\epsilon_0x$ in the degree-two column of the supported complex, with $\epsilon_0=\pm1$. The augmentation/cocycle comparison is $f_c(1-\sigma)=-c(\sigma)$, so after choosing $\sigma$ the induced $H^1\to A$ is $[c]\mapsto-\epsilon_0c(\sigma)$. The minus sign will not affect invertibility; no equality with a Gysin normalization is asserted.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text:
Consider the pairing $C(V^\vee)\otimes_A^LC(V)\to C(A)\xrightarrow b A(-1)[-1]$ induced by evaluation. The averaging projector for $S$ identifies $(V^\vee)^S$ with $(V^S)^\vee$: restrict a functional and extend back by the projector. These inverse maps are $G$-equivariant. Thus write $W_0^\vee$ for this space, with action $t^{-\mathrm{tr}}$. In degrees $(0,1)$ cup/evaluation sends an invariant functional $f$ and a crossed homomorphism $c$ to $g\mapsto f(c(g))$; in degrees $(1,0)$ it sends $d$ and invariant $v$ to $g\mapsto d(g)(v)$. This is simply functoriality of degree-one cohomology for the coefficient maps $f:V\to A$ and $v:V^\vee\to A$; the model is natural in those maps. The preceding step therefore identifies the two induced pairings, up to its nonzero sign, with
$$(W_0^\vee)^t\times W_0/(1-t)W_0\to A,\qquad W_0^\vee/(1-t^{-\mathrm{tr}})W_0^\vee\times W_0^t\to A,$$
both given by evaluation. They are perfect: the first invariant subspace is the annihilator of $(1-t)W_0$, and the image of $1-t^{-\mathrm{tr}}$ is the annihilator of $\ker(1-t)$, by the transpose equation and rank-nullity. Consequently the transpose
$$C(V^\vee)\longrightarrow R\operatorname{Hom}_A(C(V),E)[1]$$
is an isomorphism. To check this last inference, a bounded finite-dimensional complex splits as its cohomology plus contractible pairs by choosing complements to cycles and boundaries. Its derived dual has the dual cohomology, so the two perfect pairings give isomorphisms in the only cohomological degrees $0,1$.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text: Put $D=R\mathcal Hom_A(-,A_T)$. Apply the internal-Hom localization triangle to $K=i_*W$ for a finite-dimensional $A$-space $W$. Its generic term is zero and its closed restriction is $W$, by the gluing equivalence. It gives $D(i_*W)=i_*R\operatorname{Hom}_A(W,E)=i_*(W^\vee\otimes_A A(-1))[-2]$. Applying it again cancels the line and the shifts. The comparisons are induced by evaluation and adjunction; thus the bidual map restricted to $s$ is the finite-dimensional double-dual evaluation, with the Koszul shift signs, and is invertible. Explicitly choose a basis of $W$ and a nonzero basis of the line $A(-1)$; each basis vector goes to its ordinary double dual times a sign, a unit. Its generic restriction is the map between zero objects. Exact conservative geometric stalks, applied to cohomology, prove that the specified bidual map for $i_*W$ is an isomorphism.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text: For lisse $\mathscr L$ on $\eta$, apply the same internal-Hom triangle to $K=j_!\mathscr L$. Its closed restriction is zero, giving $D(j_!\mathscr L)\simeq Rj_*\mathscr L^\vee$. Here $R\mathcal Hom_A(\mathscr L,A_\eta)=\mathscr L^\vee$: on an etale cover trivializing $\mathscr L$, internal Hom is the finite direct sum of the identity functor, hence has no higher derived terms; the exact slice-restriction theorem identifies these local computations. This object is bounded constructible by step 2. The same argument applies to $\mathscr L^\vee$.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text:
Now apply the internal-Hom triangle to the bounded complex $K=Rj_*\mathscr L$. Using $i^*K=C(V)$ and $j^*K=\mathscr L$, rotate it to
$$D(Rj_*\mathscr L)\longrightarrow Rj_*\mathscr L^\vee\xrightarrow u i_*R\operatorname{Hom}_A(C(V),E)[1].$$
Both terms after the first are bounded constructible by steps 2 and 4, so the first is as well (the cohomology long exact sequence and finite-stalk closure of step 1 suffice). The boundary-pairing comparison states that $i^*u$ is the transpose of exactly the cup/evaluation/$b$ pairing of step 4, up to a unit sign. Hence $i^*u$ is an isomorphism and $i^*D(Rj_*\mathscr L)=0$. On the generic open, slice restriction of internal Hom gives $j^*D(Rj_*\mathscr L)=\mathscr L^\vee$. The open/closed extension triangle therefore identifies $D(Rj_*\mathscr L)$ with $j_!\mathscr L^\vee$. This deduction uses the boundary comparison, not merely an abstract isomorphism between cohomology spaces.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text: Steps 6 and 7, applied also to $\mathscr L^\vee$, show that both the source and target of $\eta_{j_!\mathscr L}:j_!\mathscr L\to D^2(j_!\mathscr L)$ have zero closed restriction. On the generic open the map is ordinary finite locally free double-dual evaluation: evaluation, symmetry, and transposition restrict to the same operations on the slice site, and in a local basis this is the ordinary basis-to-double-dual map. It is therefore invertible there. Exactness and conservativity of geometric stalks show that this particular $\eta$, rather than just some map between isomorphic objects, is an isomorphism.

source.place: XVII 1.2.1–1.2.3, printed pp.259–262; finite-field evaluation argument supplied here

proof.text: Every constructible sheaf $M$ has the short exact sequence $0\to j_!j^*M\to M\to i_*i^*M\to0$. It gives a distinguished triangle, with the outer terms of the types handled above. Bounded complexes are obtained by finitely many cohomological truncation triangles from their constructible cohomology sheaves. The functor $D$ is contravariantly triangulated, so the long exact cohomology sequence, finite-stalk closure from step 1, and induction over these two kinds of triangles show $D(M)\in D^b_c$ for every $M\in D^b_c$. The relative-bidual-triangles theorem says that the specified evaluation-transpose $\eta$ is natural, respects shifts and all three triangle maps, and its isomorphism locus is triangulated. The same two inductions therefore show that $\eta_M$ is invertible for every bounded constructible complex. Together with the constant sheaf's constructibility in step 1, these are precisely all three requirements in the statement. None of these steps uses completeness, mixed characteristic, a potential dualizing complex, or absolute purity.
